summary: The note examines the rise of nutritional therapy, or using food as medicine, for preventive health, and weighs the 'superfood' trend against balanced dietary patterns. Experts such as Michaela Peterson, Dr. Angela Brooks, Linda Martinez and Dr. Rebecca Li caution that no single food is a cure-all and stress dietary diversity, bio-individuality and respect for traditional diets. It also cites research linking diet, such as flavonoid-rich foods and the Mediterranean pattern, to lower chronic disease risk, and calls for evidence-based approaches over marketing hype.
one_line: Nutritional therapy and food-as-medicine trends are reviewed critically, with experts favoring balanced, diverse diets and evidence over superfood hype.
key_facts: The phrase "Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food" is attributed to Hippocrates over two millennia ago.
Registered Dietitian Michaela Peterson gave a talk on September 15, 2023, emphasizing that the way we eat has profound implications for health.
A 2023 survey by the National Health and Wellness Club found that 73% of participants believe food impacts their health significantly.
Dr. Angela Brooks, a nutrition scientist, said in a publication on October 3, 2023, that the term 'superfoods' can be misleading and does not automatically confer extraordinary health benefits.
A study published November 10, 2023, in the Journal of Functional Foods found that no single 'super' food can be a magic bullet for health and stressed a diverse, balanced diet.
The Mediterranean diet, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, nuts, whole grains and healthy fats, has been linked to reduced risk of heart disease and cognitive decline.
At a panel discussion on December 7, 2023, Dr. Simon Vega emphasized bio-individuality: what works for one person may not work for another.
Registered dietitian Linda Martinez warned in a workshop on January 12, 2024, that over-relying on kale risks nutrient imbalances or even toxicities.
A landmark study released on February 20, 2024, found that participants who ate more flavonoid-rich foods had a lower risk of heart disease.
Nutritional Anthropologist Dr. Rebecca Li said at a symposium on March 13, 2024, that many indigenous diets, plant-rich and minimally processed, embody principles now seen as scientifically sound.
Chronic diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer have been linked to dietary choices.
Rising interest in nutritional therapy has increased demand for personalized nutritional counseling and tailor-made 'food prescriptions.'
